title: Maybell Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Maybell wells have a 100 ft median depth, 11 gpm median yield, and typical finished costs of $11,000-$19,500.
h1: Maybell, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or planning a home near Maybell means understanding what nearby well records can—and cannot—tell you. Within 5 miles of Maybell, Colorado, DWR records include 234 permitted wells. Of those, 153 are recorded as constructed, 154 report total depth, 25 report pump yield, and only 4 report a static water level.

The local record is useful for setting expectations. Maybell wells have a 100-foot median depth, a median reported yield of 11.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level of 60 feet. Those figures are planning information, not a guarantee for a particular lot.

sections.heading: Maybell Well Depths Reflect Mixed Sedimentary and Alluvial Ground
sections.html:
The median Maybell well is 100 feet deep. The middle half runs from 58 to 194 feet, meaning many wells fall in that range, while the 90th percentile reaches 297 feet. The deepest well in the records is 800 feet.

Depths are split fairly broadly: 49% are under 100 feet, 41% are between 100 and 300 feet, 9% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 1% are deeper than 600 feet. For a driller's bid, that spread matters. A nearby shallow well does not prove your lot will be shallow, particularly where sediment, alluvium, and bedrock conditions change across short distances.

The permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 233 wells. Fractured rock can be unpredictable because water enters through specific fractures rather than a uniform layer.

sections.heading: Reported Maybell Yields Are Generally Useful, but Records Are Limited
sections.html:
Among the 25 Maybell wells that report a pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, 48% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 12% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a reasonable local starting point for a domestic well discussion, but the sample is much smaller than the total permit count. Yield also depends on the test method, pump setting, storage, and seasonal conditions. Ask for the well construction report and pumping information, not just a verbal production claim.

Domestic and household wells make up 60% of the permits; stock use accounts for 12%, and irrigation accounts for 1%.

sections.heading: Maybell Water Levels Have Too Little Data for a Trend Call
sections.html:
Only 4 wells in the Maybell records report a static water level, so the local water-level data is too limited to establish a reliable trend by decade. The reported median depth to water is 60 feet, with the middle half between 32 and 171 feet.

That range gives a buyer two practical warnings. First, depth to water can vary substantially between nearby wells. Second, static water level is not the same as pumping drawdown or the depth where a pump should be set. A well may have water at a relatively shallow level but still need testing to confirm that it can sustain the intended use.

Before closing, request the actual well permit and construction record for the property, then compare completed wells near the lot. A driller can use those records together with surface geology and site access to discuss likely casing, grout, and pump requirements.

sections.heading: Maybell Permit History Shows Long-Term Drilling Activity
sections.html:
Maybell has a long permit history rather than a recent burst of construction. The records show 1 permit in the 1950s, 13 in the 1970s, 56 in the 1980s, 72 in the 1990s, 31 in the 2000s, 13 in the 2010s, and 14 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active named driller in the records is Craig Drilling (Herod, James Leroy), associated with 43 wells. Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 25 records, and Visintainer Co. (Visintainer, Walter) appears on 15. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a company is still available for a new job.

For a current bid, confirm licensing, insurance, access requirements, estimated mobilization, and who will handle the permit. A driller should also explain what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than expected.

sections.heading: A Typical New Maybell Well Costs $11,000 to $19,500 Finished
sections.html:
In Maybell's mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, the drilling rate model is $50 to $75 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models at about $5,000 to $7,500.

A finished well—including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical—is modeled at about $11,000 to $19,500. That is a planning range, not a fixed quote. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, long utility runs, or challenging excavation can move the final price outside the basic estimate.

When comparing bids, ask for separate prices for drilling, casing and grout, development and testing, pump equipment, tank, electrical work, trenching, permit work, and site restoration. Also ask whether the bid includes a dry-hole policy. The difference between a drilled hole and a usable water system is substantial, so compare complete scopes rather than foot rates alone.

sections.heading: Maybell Buyers Should Check Water Quality, Septic, and Buildability
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not establish that a particular Maybell well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review environmental records and test the water before relying on it.

Low yield and dry holes remain site-specific risks even though no reported yield is under 1 gallon per minute. The permit database has more depth records than yield records, so absence of a low-yield report does not remove the risk.

Check the proposed septic area, replacement area, driveway, and house location before drilling. Confirm setbacks, soil conditions, utility routes, and whether excavation can reach the building site. If the property is in an over-appropriated basin, ask Colorado DWR whether an augmentation plan or other water-right issue affects the intended use.

sections.heading: Use Nearby Records Before Buying a Maybell Lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not the Maybell average. Pull the DWR permit and construction records for the property and compare them with completed wells nearby. Records from Craig, Meeker, Hayden, Rangely, Dinosaur, or Oak Creek may provide broader regional context, but the most useful comparisons are the wells closest to the lot and in similar ground.

For a purchase, make water a due-diligence item. Confirm the well permit, construction details, pump information, water quality testing, and any recorded limits on use. If the property has no well, get a driller's site-specific opinion and a written estimate that addresses access, likely depth, casing, pump equipment, and dry-hole terms.

If you are building, coordinate the well, septic system, access driveway, trenching, and house location before committing to plans. That prevents a water location from creating an avoidable septic or construction problem.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Maybell, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded Maybell well is 100 feet deep. The middle half ranges from 58 to 194 feet, while the 90th percentile is 297 feet. About 49% are under 100 feet and 41% are between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest recorded well is 800 feet, so a nearby shallow well is not a guarantee for your lot.

faq.q: How much water do Maybell wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 25 Maybell wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 11.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-eight percent report 5 to 15 gallons per minute, and 40% report more than 15. Because yield data covers only 25 wells, request a pumping test for the specific property.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Maybell?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 100-foot median depth, drilling the hole models at $5,000 to $7,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,000 to $19,500. Access, depth, casing, grout, and site conditions can change the quote.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Maybell?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that any individual Maybell well is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 5 historic mine features, and 4 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the water from the specific well for relevant contaminants, and review nearby environmental records before relying on it.

faq.q: Are Maybell wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available records do not support a reliable water-level trend because only 4 wells report static water levels. Those reported levels have a median depth to water of 60 feet, with a middle half from 32 to 171 feet. This does not predict future performance. Check the specific well's construction, pumping history, seasonal behavior, and nearby completed wells.
